facts.statement: Cartorhynchus lived during the Early Triassic epoch, approximately 248 million years ago.
facts.quote: Cartorhynchus (meaning "shortened snout") is an extinct genus of early ichthyosauriform marine reptile that lived during the Early Triassic epoch, about 248 million years ago.

facts.statement: The specimen was assigned the field number MT-II and the specimen number AGB 6257 at the Anhui Geological Museum.
facts.quote: It received a field number of MT-II, and later a specimen number of AGB 6257 at the Anhui Geological Museum.

facts.statement: Ryosuke Motani and colleagues described the specimen as a new genus and species, Cartorhynchus lenticarpus, in Nature in 2014.
facts.quote: In 2014, the specimen was described by Ryosuke Motani and colleagues in Nature as representing a new genus and species, Cartorhynchus lenticarpus.

facts.statement: Jian-Dong Huang, Motani, and colleagues used micro-CT scanning performed at the Yinghua Testing Company in Shanghai to examine the interior of the jaws because the specimen was too fragile to open.
facts.quote: Since the specimen was too fragile to expose the interior of the jaws, Jian-Dong Huang, Motani, and other colleagues subsequently scanned and rendered the specimen in 3D using micro-computed tomography (micro-CT), performed at the Yinghua Testing Company in Shanghai, China.

facts.statement: Cartorhynchus was a small animal measuring about 40 cm in length with a lizard-like body and short torso.
facts.quote: Measuring about 40 cm long, Cartorhynchus was a small animal with a lizard-like body and a short torso

facts.statement: Cartorhynchus had limbs with extensive cartilage that could bend like flippers, possibly allowing it to walk on land.
facts.quote: Its limbs bore extensive cartilage and could bend like flippers, which may have allowed it to walk on land.

facts.statement: Cartorhynchus is characterized by a short, constricted snout and multiple rows of molar-like teeth growing on the inner surface of its jaw bones.
facts.quote: The most distinctive features of Cartorhynchus were its short, constricted snout and its multiple rows of molar-like teeth which grew on the inside surface of its jaw bones.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Cartorhynchus preyed on hard-shelled invertebrates using suction feeding, though the exact mechanism of its inward-directed teeth remains unknown.
facts.quote: Cartorhynchus likely preyed on hard-shelled invertebrates using suction feeding, although how it exactly used its inward-directed teeth is not yet known.

facts.statement: At the time of its discovery, Cartorhynchus was the smallest known member of the Ichthyosauriformes.
facts.quote: At the time of its discovery, Cartorhynchus was the smallest-known member of the Ichthyosauriformes.

facts.statement: In 2021, Sander and colleagues estimated the weight of Cartorhynchus to be 237 g.
facts.quote: In 2021, Sander and colleagues produced a much lower weight estimate of 237 g.

facts.statement: Cartorhynchus possessed an unusually short snout occupying half the skull's length and a deep jaw.
facts.quote: Cartorhynchus had an unusually short and constricted snout, which occupied only half of the skull's length, and a deep jaw.

facts.statement: The tip of the Cartorhynchus snout was only 6 mm wide.
facts.quote: The tip of the snout was only 6 mm wide.

facts.statement: Unlike most reptiles, the nasal bone of Cartorhynchus extended to the front of the snout.
facts.quote: Unlike most reptiles, its nasal bone reached the front of the snout.

facts.statement: The teeth of Cartorhynchus were either completely flattened or weakly pointed, with many bearing a constriction between the root and crown.
facts.quote: All of the teeth were either completely flattened or weakly pointed, and many of the teeth bore a constriction between the root and the crown.

facts.statement: Cartorhynchus teeth were arranged in three rows on the upper and lower jawbones, with the outermost row containing the most and largest teeth.
facts.quote: On the maxilla (upper jawbone) and dentary (lower jawbone), the teeth were arranged in three rows, with the outermost row having the most and largest teeth

facts.statement: Among ichthyosauriforms, only Cartorhynchus and Xinminosaurus possess multiple rows of teeth.
facts.quote: Among ichthyosauriforms, only Cartorhynchus and Xinminosaurus have multiple rows of teeth.

facts.statement: The limbs of Cartorhynchus were poorly ossified, with only three hand digits ossified and widely spaced bones, suggesting extensive cartilage.
facts.quote: The limbs of Cartorhynchus were poorly ossified (only three digits of the hand were ossified) with widely-spaced bones, particularly between the wrist bones (carpals) and the digits, suggesting the presence of extensive cartilage in the limbs.

facts.statement: Cartorhynchus was part of a rapid diversification of marine reptiles during the Spathian substage, occurring about one million years after the Permian-Triassic extinction event.
facts.quote: Along with its close relative Sclerocormus, Cartorhynchus was part of a diversification of marine reptiles that occurred suddenly (over about one million years) during the Spathian substage, soon after the devastating Permian-Triassic extinction event

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the inability of the lower jaw bones to fuse tightly in Cartorhynchus was a characteristic shared with toothless hupehsuchians.
facts.quote: This characteristic would have been shared with its close relatives, the toothless hupehsuchians.

facts.statement: Cartorhynchus belongs to the clade Nasorostra, which is the sister group to Ichthyopterygia.
facts.quote: Phylogenetic analyses conducted by Motani and colleagues found that the two were closely related to each other — forming a clade (group) called the Nasorostra — and to the Ichthyopterygia, to which nasorostrans formed the sister group.

facts.statement: In 2014, researchers named the group containing Cartorhynchus and Ichthyopterygia Ichthyosauriformes, and the larger group including Hupehsuchia Ichthyosauromorpha.
facts.quote: In 2014, Motani and colleagues named the clade formed by Nasorostra and Ichthyopterygia as the Ichthyosauriformes, and the clade formed by Ichthyosauriformes and Hupehsuchia as the Ichthyosauromorpha.

facts.statement: Cartorhynchus possessed molariform teeth, indicating a diet that included hard-shelled animals.
facts.quote: Many ichthyosauriforms from the Early and Middle Triassic had molariform teeth (shown in the phylogenetic tree above), including Cartorhynchus; such teeth indicate a diet at least partially based on hard-shelled animals.

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesized in 2014 that Cartorhynchus was a suction feeder.
facts.quote: Motani and colleagues hypothesized in 2014 that Cartorhynchus was a suction feeder which fed by concentrating pressure in its narrow snout.

facts.statement: A 2020 study concluded that Cartorhynchus was a durophagous feeder based on its molariform teeth.
facts.quote: The discovery of molariform teeth in Cartorhynchus led Huang and colleagues to conclude in 2020 that Cartorhynchus was durophagous, feeding on hard-shelled prey.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that despite being durophagous, Cartorhynchus was likely restricted to feeding on small prey.
facts.quote: However, they suggested that Cartorhynchus would have been restricted to feeding on small prey.

facts.statement: Researchers proposed that the unusual wear patterns on Cartorhynchus teeth might be due to jaw twisting during preservation or the loss of soft tissues, though neither fully explains the evidence.
facts.quote: They noted that teeth are structurally strongest at their tips, not on their sides, under the high stresses of crushing bites. They suggested that the jaw may have been twisted during preservation, or soft tissues like collagen which held up the teeth in life may have been lost, although they conceded that neither hypothesis would explain the wear patterns.

facts.statement: Cartorhynchus had poorly ossified limbs despite having a well-ossified skull and vertebrae.
facts.quote: Cartorhynchus had poorly ossified limbs in spite of its well-ossified skull and vertebrae.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested Cartorhynchus was an adult exhibiting paedomorphosis, but acknowledged the possibility it was a juvenile given only one specimen exists.
facts.quote: However, Motani and colleagues suggested in 2014 that it was still an adult because many early-diverging members of marine reptile lineages have poorly-ossified limbs through paedomorphosis (the retention of immature traits into adulthood), although they did not completely reject the possibility that it was a juvenile due to the existence of only one specimen.

facts.statement: The extensive cartilage at Cartorhynchus's wrist joint likely allowed its flippers to bend without an elbow, similar to juvenile sea turtles.
facts.quote: The extensive cartilage at the wrist joint would have allowed the flipper to bend without an elbow; juvenile sea turtles have similarly cartilaginous flippers that they use to move on land.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested Cartorhynchus had an amphibious lifestyle aided by a short trunk, snout, and thickened ribs acting as ballast.
facts.quote: Motani and colleagues suggested that other traits of Cartorhynchus would also have aided an amphibious lifestyle, including the short trunk and snout, and the thickened ribs (which would have served as a ballast, stabilizing the animal in near-shore waters).

facts.statement: Cartorhynchus lived approximately 248.41 million years ago.
facts.quote: Bed 633 in particular was estimated at 248.41 Ma in age.

facts.statement: Cartorhynchus lived in an oceanic basin located relatively far from the coast during the Middle Triassic.
facts.quote: During the Middle Triassic, the Chaohu strata were deposited in an oceanic basin relatively far from the coast
